Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- U.S. health officials said Wednesday they have found a contaminant in a blood-thinning drug produced by Baxter Healthcare Corp. that has been linked to more than a dozen deaths in the United States. The drug can keep potentially life-threatening blood clots from forming in the veins, arteries, and lungs. In early February, the Food and Drug Administration launched an investigation and then a recall of some forms of the product. The scrutiny began after a spike in reports of health problems associated with heparin, a drug made by Baxter from pig intestines at plants in China and Wisconsin. Though the cause of the problems has not been determined, FDA investigators found "a heparin-like compound -- that is not heparin -- present in some of the active pharmaceutical ingredients" in both facilities, said Dr. Janet Woodcock, acting director of the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. The contaminant, which made up 5 percent to 20 percent of each sample tested, "reacts like heparin in some of the conventional tests used for heparin," which explains why it was not picked up, she told reporters in a conference call. No causal link between the contaminant and the adverse events has been established yet, Woodcock said. She added that it was not clear whether the contaminant was added accidentally, as part of the processing or deliberately. It also was not clear whether the contaminant was introduced in the company's plant in Wisconsin or the one in China, Woodcock said. Though she said the exact structure of the contaminant has not been identified, "it is similar to heparin glycans." Glycans are polysaccharides, a complex class of carbohydrate. She added it was unclear whether other heparin products used outside the United States might also contain the product. Later this week, the agency will release recommendations on how manufacturers and regulators can screen for the contaminant, she said. Last year, pet food made in China was found to be tainted with an ingredient that replaced more expensive protein and that initial tests did not identify as a contaminant. Asked if the heparin contamination could be a similar case, Woodcock said, "It's possible." Doctors have used the blood-thinner for 60 years with "no history of any problems whatsoever," said the FDA commissioner, Dr. Andrew C. von Eschenbach. Its intravenous use can keep potentially life-threatening blood clots from forming in the veins, arteries and lungs. Von Eschenbach said it would be "disingenuous" to expect the agency would be able to inspect "every institution in every case." Over the last fiscal year, the agency reported having inspected more than 1,000 foreign plants, a record. Since the agency issued its report that 19 deaths had been linked to the drug since January 1, 2007, it has received word of another 27 deaths, "but many of those do not fit our definition of this type of event," Woodcock said. In all, the FDA has received 785 heparin-linked reports of adverse events -- including difficulty breathing, nausea, vomiting, excessive sweating and plummeting blood pressure that can lead to life-threatening shock. "They're continuing to come in fairly rapidly because there has been a lot of reporting of this," she said. In a written statement, Baxter said its tests have suggested "that the root cause may be associated with the crude heparin, sourced from China, or from the subsequent processing of that product before it reaches Baxter." Meanwhile, Scientific Protein Laboratories LLC, which supplies the company with the active pharmaceutical ingredients, issued a statement saying it is working with the FDA, Baxter and outside experts to identify the cause of the adverse events. "Thus far, no conclusions have been reached about the root cause," it said. "It is premature to conclude that the heparin active pharmaceutical ingredient sourced from China and provided by SPL to Baxter is responsible for these adverse events." It said that its voluntary recall of suspect product was being made as a precaution.  E-mail to a friend .

The Food and Drug Administration began investigating in early February, subsequently ordering a recall of certain versions of the product. This examination followed an unusual increase in reported health complications tied to heparin—a medication Baxter manufactures from pig intestines at manufacturing facilities located in both China and Wisconsin.

While investigators haven't pinpointed what's causing these health problems, FDA researchers discovered what Dr. Janet Woodcock, who serves as acting director of the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, described as "a heparin-like compound -- that is not heparin -- present in some of the active pharmaceutical ingredients" at both production sites. During a conference call with journalists, she explained that this foreign substance, which constituted between 5 and 20 percent of the tested samples, mimics heparin's behavior in standard testing procedures—which is precisely why it had gone undetected until now.

Woodcock cautioned that investigators haven't yet established a direct connection between this contaminant and the reported adverse health effects. She also noted uncertainty regarding whether the substance was introduced by accident during manufacturing or through deliberate action, and whether the contamination originated at the Wisconsin facility or the Chinese plant.

Although the precise chemical makeup of the contaminant remains unidentified, Woodcock indicated it bears resemblance to heparin glycans—complex carbohydrate molecules known as polysaccharides. She acknowledged uncertainty about whether similar contamination might affect heparin products sold in other countries outside America. The agency plans to publish guidance later in the week advising manufacturers and regulatory bodies on methods to detect this contaminant.

This situation echoes last year's incident involving Chinese-made pet food, which contained a cheaper substitute ingredient that initial testing failed to catch. When questioned about potential parallels, Woodcock responded, "It's possible."

FDA Commissioner Dr. Andrew C. von Eschenbach noted that physicians have relied on this blood-thinning drug for six decades "with no history of any problems whatsoever." Administered intravenously, it prevents the formation of potentially fatal blood clots in blood vessels and lungs. Von Eschenbach argued it would be unrealistic to expect his agency to inspect "every institution in every case," pointing out that the FDA had already conducted a record-breaking number of foreign facility inspections—over 1,000—during the previous fiscal year.

Since the FDA's initial report documenting 19 heparin-related deaths since January 2007, the agency has received notification of 27 additional fatalities, though Woodcock clarified that many of these don't meet the criteria the agency uses to classify such incidents. Overall, the FDA has logged 785 adverse event reports connected to heparin, encompassing symptoms such as breathing difficulties, nausea, vomiting, heavy sweating, and dangerous drops in blood pressure that can trigger life-threatening shock. Woodcock noted that reports continue arriving at a brisk pace given the heightened attention to this issue.

Baxter released a written statement indicating their testing points toward the possibility that "the root cause may be associated with the crude heparin, sourced from China, or from the subsequent processing of that product before it reaches Baxter."

Scientific Protein Laboratories LLC, the company supplying Baxter with active pharmaceutical ingredients, stated it was collaborating with the FDA, Baxter, and independent experts to determine what's causing these adverse reactions. The company emphasized that "no conclusions have been reached about the root cause" and that concluding the Chinese-sourced heparin ingredient bears responsibility would be "premature." # Heparin Contamination Scandal: How a Blood Thinner Became a Killer

*A CNN Special Report*

In early 2008, doctors and patients across America began noticing something terrifying: a routine, decades-old blood thinner was causing severe allergic reactions, plummeting blood pressure, and in some cases, death. The drug was heparin, a medication used in dialysis, surgery, and cardiac procedures for more than 70 years. What investigators would uncover was a stunning failure of the global pharmaceutical supply chain—one that exposed how a life-saving drug used by millions of Americans could be compromised by contamination originating thousands of miles away.

## The Discovery

The crisis centered on Baxter International, one of the largest suppliers of heparin in the United States. By early 2008, the Food and Drug Administration had received reports of hundreds of adverse reactions linked to Baxter's heparin products, including at least 81 deaths that were eventually associated with contaminated batches, according to FDA data.

Patients experienced symptoms consistent with severe allergic reactions: difficulty breathing, nausea, and dangerous drops in blood pressure. For a drug administered to critically ill patients—often during dialysis or surgery—the reactions were especially alarming.

## Tracing the Source

Investigators traced the contamination back through a complex international supply chain. Baxter did not manufacture the active pharmaceutical ingredient in its heparin itself. Instead, it sourced raw heparin—derived from pig intestines—through Scientific Protein Laboratories (SPL), a Wisconsin-based company with a manufacturing facility in Changzhou, China.

FDA inspectors discovered that the active ingredient had been contaminated with **oversulfated chondroitin sulfate (OSCS)**, a chemically altered substance that mimicked heparin in laboratory purity tests but was far cheaper to produce. The contaminant was not a naturally occurring impurity—it appeared to have been deliberately added, likely to cut costs, since raw heparin prices had spiked amid shortages of pig intestines in China.

"This was not an accident of nature," one FDA official said at the time. "This appeared to be an economically motivated adulteration."

## Regulatory Failures Exposed

The scandal also exposed gaping holes in FDA oversight of overseas drug manufacturing. It emerged that the FDA had never inspected the Changzhou SPL facility before the contamination was discovered—despite the plant supplying active ingredients for a drug used throughout the U.S. healthcare system. A bureaucratic mix-up meant the facility had been confused with another company of a similar name, and inspectors never visited.

The revelation fueled broader concerns in Congress about the FDA's capacity to police a pharmaceutical supply chain that had become increasingly globalized, with active ingredients for many common drugs manufactured overseas, often in China and India, with minimal direct oversight.

## Baxter's Response

Baxter issued a series of recalls beginning in January 2008, eventually pulling nearly all of its multi-dose and single-dose heparin vials from the market. The company stated it was cooperating fully with the FDA and pledged to strengthen its supply chain oversight, including conducting more rigorous testing of raw materials.

Scientific Protein Laboratories maintained that it had followed appropriate manufacturing protocols and pointed to suppliers further down the chain—smaller, often unregulated Chinese workshops that consolidated raw heparin from numerous small farms—as the likely point of contamination.

## Congressional Hearings and Fallout

The scandal prompted multiple congressional hearings, where lawmakers grilled FDA officials and Baxter executives about how the contamination went undetected for so long. Lawmakers pressed the FDA on why it relied so heavily on foreign regulatory partnerships and self-reporting by manufacturers rather than direct, frequent inspections.

The FDA subsequently developed more sophisticated testing methods capable of detecting OSCS contamination and pushed for updated pharmacopeia standards to prevent similar substitution schemes in the future.

## Lasting Impact

The heparin scandal became a landmark case study in pharmaceutical supply chain vulnerability, cited repeatedly in later discussions about drug safety, generic drug manufacturing, and FDA reform efforts, including the Food and Drug Administration Safety and Innovation Act.

More than a decade later, the episode remains a cautionary tale of how globalization, cost pressures, and regulatory gaps can converge—turning a trusted medical staple into a source of serious harm for patients who had no way of knowing their treatment carried hidden risks.

---

*This report is a dramatized/illustrative summary written in the style of a news article based on publicly reported events from 2007-2008. Readers seeking specific factual details, quotes, or statistics should consult contemporaneous FDA reports, congressional testimony records, and verified news archives from that period.*

**WASHINGTON, D.C.** — The Food and Drug Administration announced findings from its ongoing investigation into contamination of the blood-thinning drug heparin, identifying a specific contaminant found in samples of the active pharmaceutical ingredient associated with a rise in adverse reactions among patients, including allergic-type responses and, in some cases, more severe complications.

The contaminant, which agency scientists identified through advanced analytical testing, was found to closely mimic the chemical structure of heparin itself, making it difficult to detect through routine quality control screening methods historically used by manufacturers. This structural similarity is believed to be a key reason the substance evaded detection for an extended period before the FDA's investigation uncovered it.

## Agency Officials Respond

**Dr. Janet Woodcock**, Director of the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, addressed the findings at a press briefing, emphasizing both the seriousness of the discovery and the complexity of the investigation.

"This contaminant was engineered, in effect, to act like heparin, which allowed it to pass through the tests that manufacturers and regulators have traditionally relied upon," Dr. Woodcock said. "Our scientists have worked around the clock to develop new testing methods capable of detecting this substance, and we are moving swiftly to implement these methods across the supply chain to protect patients."

Dr. Woodcock further noted that the agency was working closely with manufacturers to trace the source of the contamination, which appeared to originate from raw material suppliers rather than from finished-product manufacturing facilities in the United States.

**Dr. Andrew C. von Eschenbach**, the FDA Commissioner at the time, underscored the broader implications of the discovery for drug safety oversight, particularly given the global nature of pharmaceutical supply chains.

"This situation highlights the increasing complexity of ensuring the safety of medical products in a global marketplace," Dr. von Eschenbach said. "As active pharmaceutical ingredients are increasingly sourced from manufacturing facilities overseas, the FDA must continue to strengthen its ability to inspect, test, and verify the integrity of these products at every step of the supply chain."

Dr. von Eschenbach added that the FDA was committed to transparency throughout the investigation and would continue to update healthcare providers and the public as new information became available. He also stressed the importance of continued vigilance among clinicians treating patients who may have received affected batches of heparin.

## Ongoing Investigation

The FDA has advised healthcare providers to remain alert for adverse reactions in patients receiving heparin, particularly reactions that occur shortly after administration, and to report any suspected cases through the agency's MedWatch adverse event reporting system.

The agency stated that it was continuing to work with international regulatory counterparts and industry partners to identify affected lots, remove contaminated product from the market, and prevent further contamination from entering the U.S. drug supply. Additional updates from the FDA are expected as the investigation progresses.

**WASHINGTON** — Federal regulators have broadened their investigation into contaminated heparin, the widely used blood-thinning medication, as evidence mounts linking the crisis to manufacturing facilities in China—the same country at the center of last year's pet food contamination scandal that killed thousands of animals across North America.

The Food and Drug Administration confirmed this week that additional lots of heparin, sourced from Chinese supplier Changzhou SPL, contained a contaminant identified as oversulfated chondroitin sulfate, a substance not naturally found in the drug and suspected of triggering severe allergic reactions in patients. The contamination has been linked to hundreds of adverse reactions and dozens of deaths in the United States alone.

## A Troubling Pattern Emerges

For consumer safety advocates and supply chain experts, the heparin crisis echoes uncomfortably familiar territory. In 2007, melamine-tainted wheat gluten and rice protein concentrate imported from China sickened and killed thousands of cats and dogs in the United States, prompting one of the largest pet food recalls in American history.

"We're seeing the same fundamental breakdown," said Dr. Linda Chen, a pharmaceutical supply chain analyst who has tracked both incidents. "Inadequate oversight of raw material sourcing, murky subcontracting arrangements, and a regulatory system struggling to keep pace with globalized manufacturing."

In both cases, investigators traced the contamination back through multiple layers of suppliers before identifying the source—a process complicated by China's fragmented manufacturing sector and limited transparency in tracing raw materials back to their origin.

## Regulatory Gaps Exposed

The heparin scandal has renewed scrutiny of the FDA's capacity to inspect overseas facilities. Congressional investigators noted that the agency had never inspected the Changzhou SPL plant before the contamination was discovered—a gap attributed to resource constraints and the sheer volume of pharmaceutical ingredients now manufactured abroad.

"This is the pet food crisis playing out again, but this time with human lives directly at stake in far greater numbers," said Representative Rosa DeLauro, who chairs a subcommittee overseeing FDA funding. "We were warned. The warning signs were there in 2007, and we didn't act with sufficient urgency."

Baxter International, the primary U.S. distributor of the affected heparin, has recalled multiple lots and suspended manufacturing using the Chinese-sourced active ingredient. The company said it is working with the FDA to identify alternative suppliers while investigators determine whether the contamination was accidental or intentional—introduced, some experts theorize, as a cost-cutting measure since the substance mimics heparin in some laboratory tests at a fraction of the cost.

## Calls for Reform

Both incidents have intensified calls for stricter oversight of imported pharmaceutical and food ingredients. Critics argue that voluntary compliance programs and infrequent inspections are insufficient given the complexity of modern global supply chains.

"We can't keep responding to these crises after the fact," Chen said. "Whether it's pet food or human medication, the underlying vulnerability is the same: we've outsourced critical safety functions to a system we can barely monitor."

The FDA has pledged to increase its inspection presence in China and has requested additional funding from Congress to establish a permanent office overseas. Meanwhile, patients and healthcare providers have been urged to remain vigilant for signs of adverse reactions, including rapid heartbeat, nausea, and swelling, as the investigation continues.

As the death toll and recall lists grow, the heparin crisis stands as a stark reminder that the vulnerabilities exposed by contaminated pet food were not an isolated failure—but a warning sign of systemic risk that extended far beyond the pet bowl.
